_meta: One shared record (an inventory count) that two clients update concurrently by reading it, computing a new value, and writing it back, used to show that a blind read-modify-write loses one update and that a compare-and-swap on a version (optimistic concurrency control) prevents it. Both clients read the same starting value at the same version, each applies its own change, and each writes back. If the write is blind -- it just overwrites whatever is stored -- then the second writer overwrites the first writer's change without ever seeing it, so one update silently vanishes: the record ends where the second writer put it, not where both changes would have left it. This is the lost-update problem, and it happens whenever a read and a later write are not atomic and something else wrote in between. Optimistic concurrency control fixes it without holding a lock: the client remembers the version it read and includes it in the write as an expected version; the store accepts the write only if the record is still at that version (a compare-and-swap), and rejects it otherwise. The rejected client has learned its read was stale, so it re-reads the now-current value and re-applies its change, and this time its write is against the fresh version and succeeds -- so both changes land. initial_value and initial_version describe the record; client_a_delta and client_b_delta are the two concurrent changes, applied in the order A then B. The blind final value (with a lost update) and the compare-and-swap final value (correct after a retry) are computed. Stdlib only.
